## Problem 1

Simulated birthdays for groups of 2-50 people and estimated the probability of at least one shared birthday using 10,000 simulations per group size

```{r}
shared_birthday = function(n) {

  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)

  any(duplicated(birthdays))

}

birthday_results =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    shared = map_lgl(group_size, shared_birthday)
  )

birthday_summary =
  birthday_results |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(
    probability = mean(shared),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r, birthday_plot}
birthday_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of at least one shared birthday",
    x = "Number of people",
    y = "Estimated probability"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r, shared_birthday_examples, include=FALSE}
birthday_summary |>
  filter(group_size %in% c(2, 25, 50))
```

Across 10,000 simulations per group size, the estimated probability of at least one shared birthday increased with group size. For example, the probability was 0.28% with 2 people, 57.5% with 25 people, and 96.8% with 50 people. This occurs because larger groups contain more pairs of people who could share a birthday.


## Problem 2

Combined the participant files into a "tidy" dataset with 1 row per participant/week and plotted individual trajectories by study arm

```{r, tidy_data}

# Create a tidy dataframe containing data from all participants
study_df =
  tibble(
    file_name = list.files(
      path = "data",
      pattern = "\\.csv$"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    data = purrr::map(
      file_name,
      \(file) read_csv(str_c("data/", file))
    )
  )

# Extract arm and subject ID, combine data, and "tidy" weekly observations
study_tidy =
  study_df |>
  mutate(
    file_name = str_replace(file_name, "\\.csv$", "")
  ) |>
  separate(
    file_name,
    into = c("arm", "subject_id"),
    sep = "_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    arm = recode(
      arm,
      con = "Control",
      exp = "Experimental"
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.integer(week)
  )

study_tidy
```

```{r spaghetti_plot}
study_tidy |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = interaction(arm, subject_id),
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Participant observations over time",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

```

Observations in the control and experimental arms followed different trajectories over the eight-week period. The experimental arm generally showed increasing observations, while the control arm remained relatively stable with no consistent trend. The groups overlapped initially but became more separated at later weeks, with higher observations in the experimental arm. Both groups showed variation between participants and week-to-week fluctuations within participants.

## Problem 3

Generated 5,000 normally distributed datasets for each true mean from 0 to 6, fixing the sample size at 30 and standard deviation at 5, and applied a two-sided one-sample t-test against a null mean of zero.

```{r, ttest_function}
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {

  sim_data =
    tibble(
      x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
    )

  t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(
      mu_hat = estimate,
      p_value = p.value
    )

}

sim_t_test(mu = 0)
```

```{r, ttest_simulation}
t_test_results =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = results) |>
  mutate(
    rejected = p_value < 0.05
  )

t_test_results
```

```{r, power_summary}
power_summary =
  t_test_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    rejection_rate = mean(rejected),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

power_summary
```

```{r, power_plot}
power_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = rejection_rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rejection probability by true population mean",
    x = "True population mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests rejecting the null"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

With sample size and standard deviation fixed, power increased as the true population mean moved further from the null value of 0, corresponding to a larger effect size. For example, power was `r round(100 * power_summary$rejection_rate[power_summary$true_mu == 1], 1)`% at a true mean of 1, `r round(100 * power_summary$rejection_rate[power_summary$true_mu == 2], 1)`% at 2, and `r round(100 * power_summary$rejection_rate[power_summary$true_mu == 3], 1)`% at 3, approaching 100% for true means ≥4. Larger effects were therefore more likely to be detected with the same sample size and variability. When the true mean was 0, `r round(100 * power_summary$rejection_rate[power_summary$true_mu == 0], 2)`% of tests rejected the null, close to the expected Type I error rate of 5%.

```{r, mu_estimate_summary}
estimate_summary =
  t_test_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_all = mean(mu_hat),
    mean_rejected = mean(mu_hat[rejected]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

estimate_summary
```

```{r mu_estimate_plot}
estimate_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_all, mean_rejected),
    names_to = "samples",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    samples = recode(
      samples,
      mean_all = "All samples",
      mean_rejected = "Rejected null only"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = true_mu,
      y = average_estimate,
      color = samples
    )
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Average estimated mean by true population mean",
    subtitle = "Dashed line indicates equality with the true mean",
    x = "True population mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Across all simulated datasets, the average estimated mean was close to the true mean. Among datasets that rejected the null (p < 0.05), small positive effects were overestimated. For example, when the true mean was 1, the average estimate among significant datasets was `r round(estimate_summary$mean_rejected[estimate_summary$true_mu == 1], 2)`. Because sample means vary across datasets, selecting only significant results favors higher estimates and raises the average above the true mean. As power increased, nearly all datasets rejected the null, and the average estimate approached the true mean. When the true mean was 0, positive and negative significant estimates tended to cancel out, leaving an average close to zero both for all samples and for the rejected null subset.
